LESSON 76 OF 106·Social Engineering and the Human Factor

Insider Threat: Motive, Opportunity and Detection

Insider risk as the authorities actually define it: who counts as an insider, why most insider incidents are not malicious, and how to build controls that detect harm without punishing accidents.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

The phrase insider threat covers several different situations, and lumping them together leads to bad controls. Malicious insiders and negligent insiders need entirely different responses.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Motive, opportunity and capability are the three factors, and opportunity is the one an organisation controls directly.
  • Most insider incidents are accidental or negligent rather than malicious, and that changes the whole response.
  • A departing employee with abrupt behaviour, or one with a grievance, is a recognised risk signal.
  • Over-broad access makes every mistake and every malicious act far more damaging.
  • Detection usually comes from a behaviour change relative to a baseline, not from a single action.

The background

  • Early monitoring was limited to what an employee did with a file, which missed data sent to personal accounts.
  • Data loss prevention tools expanded visibility to email, removable media and cloud uploads.
  • Analytic platforms made it possible to baseline normal behaviour and alert on deviation.
  • Legal and privacy constraints in several jurisdictions limit how far behavioural monitoring can go, which is a genuine constraint.

Real-world examples

  • An employee copying a customer database to a personal drive before resigning is one of the most common insider data events.
  • A well-meaning administrator bulk-exporting data for a migration creates the same exposure with no intent at all.
  • A shared account means an insider action cannot be attributed, which blocks the investigation entirely.

What to look for

  • Check who can reach sensitive data, and whether that matches their current role rather than their history.
  • Check whether access is removed promptly and automatically when a person changes role or leaves.
  • Check whether bulk data movement is visible and alerted on.
  • Check whether actions can be attributed to a person, since shared accounts defeat this.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Detecting and Identifying Insider Threats

Reading the official US position on insider threat detection, including why both human observation and technology are required

Open CISA resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Apply least privilege continuously, so no single person can take data they have no business touching.
  • Remove access automatically on the leaver trigger, and make exceptions visible.
  • Use unique individual accounts everywhere, including for administrators.
  • Alert on bulk export and on access to data the person does not normally need.
  • Handle the negligent case with better tooling and clearer rules, since that is where the majority of incidents are.
